title: Maxwell’s Equations: Electromagnetic Waves Predicted and Observed
lead: Everything in this chapter rests on four statements that James Clerk Maxwell drew together from the work of Oersted, Coulomb, Gauss and Faraday, and on the one hypothesis about a changing electric field that he added to them. This section reads the four equations, follows what Maxwell predicted from them, and turns to Heinrich Hertz, who built the apparatus to test that prediction.
summary_html:
• Electromagnetic waves consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields and propagate at the speed of light $\kc$. They were predicted by Maxwell, who also showed that $$\kc = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}},$$ where $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space and $\varepsilon_0$ is the permittivity of free space.
  • Maxwell’s prediction of electromagnetic waves resulted from his formulation of a complete and symmetric theory of electricity and magnetism, known as Maxwell’s equations.
  • These four equations are paraphrased in this text, rather than presented numerically, and encompass the major laws of electricity and magnetism. First is Gauss’s law for electricity, second is Gauss’s law for magnetism, third is Faraday’s law of induction, including Lenz’s law, and fourth is Ampere’s law in a symmetric formulation that adds another source of magnetism—changing electric fields.
notes: The two problems the book leaves without a keyed answer are left out: the one that asks for the value of the speed of light to be verified from the permeability and the permittivity of free space, and the one that asks for the units of the same expression to be shown to be m/s.
exercise_notes: The module sets two problems and no conceptual question, no AP item and no Check Your Understanding box, and the book keys neither problem, so neither is set here: one asks the reader to verify the value of $\kc$ from $\mu_0$ and $\varepsilon_0$, and the other to verify that the units of the right-hand side of the same equation are m/s. Answers come from the book’s answer key and are never computed here, so the five concepts this section introduces are reached again by the problems of 24.2 and 24.3, which rest on them.

figures.original_caption: The apparatus used by Hertz in 1887 to generate and detect electromagnetic waves. An $\text{RLC}$ circuit connected to the first loop caused sparks across a gap in the wire loop and generated electromagnetic waves. Sparks across a gap in the second loop located across the laboratory gave evidence that the waves had been received.
